title: State of the climate: Rapidly developing El Niño raises chance of record-warm 2026 - Carbon Brief
gist: Carbon Brief's mid-2026 state-of-the-climate update finds the chance of 2026 setting a new global temperature record has nearly doubled to 35% since April on the back of an unusually fast-developing 'super' El Niño (Niño3.4 above 2C by July), a record European June heatwave, and near-record-low Arctic sea ice — with 2027 flagged as the more likely record year (92% chance) once El Niño's full warming effect lands.

themes.theme: Odds of a 2026 temperature record have nearly doubled

insights.claim: Carbon Brief's April 2026 assessment gave 2026 a 19% chance of setting a new global temperature record; that chance has nearly doubled to 35% by mid-July, with virtually all of the change driven by strengthening El Niño forecasts rather than observed temperatures.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: The signal to track for a 2026 record is the El Niño forecast trajectory, not year-to-date temperature readings, since the forecast revision is what is driving the probability shift.
insights.locator: opening paragraphs

insights.claim: Around 84% of the 28-percentage-point rise in 2026 record odds since March comes from successive upward revisions to the El Niño forecast, while the year-to-date temperature anomaly actually drifted slightly down, from 1.41C after March to 1.39C after June.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Isolates forecast-driven risk from realized-data risk, a methodological point relevant to anyone building probabilistic climate-record models.
insights.locator: Observed temperatures and fewer remaining months

themes.theme: 2026 is on a record-onset pace for El Niño itself

insights.claim: The Niño3.4 index, the standard measure of El Niño strength, crossed the 0.5C threshold in April, reached 1C in May and hit 1.6C ('strong') in June — one of the fastest El Niño onsets in the observational record — and shot above 2C in the first weeks of July.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: The onset speed itself is a record-relevant fact: fast-developing El Niños have historically preceded exceptionally warm following years.
insights.locator: A record-breaking El Niño

insights.claim: Carbon Brief's analysis of the median of 667 model runs from 14 modelling groups projects the Niño3.4 sea-surface-temperature anomaly could peak at 3.59C between July and December 2026, with over 91% of runs projecting the strongest El Niño event in the modern record, surpassing the prior 2015-16 peak of 2.75C.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: The 'super El Niño' scenario is now the model-consensus base case rather than a tail risk, relevant for anyone pricing 2026-27 weather-driven commodity or insurance exposure.
insights.locator: An analysis by Carbon Brief

insights.claim: Raw model Niño3.4 forecasts tend to overstate El Niño strength because they are measured against a fixed historical climatology while the whole tropical ocean has warmed from greenhouse gases; using the bias-corrected relative Niño3.4 index (RONI), the median forecast peak is a lower 3.1C, still above the prior RONI record of 2.69C set in 1982-83, with 77% of model runs still projecting a new record event.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Gives the more rigorous, bias-adjusted probability (77%) for a record El Niño, which should be preferred over the raw, unadjusted model read.
insights.locator: A cleaner comparison uses

insights.claim: Model El Niño forecasts issued in spring and early summer have historically shown some bias toward overpredicting eventual event strength, but forecasts issued after spring are considerably more reliable.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Increases confidence in the current mid-July forecast and the associated 35% record-odds estimate, since it postdates the less-reliable spring forecasting window.
insights.locator: Model forecasts made in the spring

themes.theme: First half of 2026 in the historical record

insights.claim: The first six months of 2026 were the third-warmest start to a year on record across all six major global temperature datasets, at around 1.4C above pre-industrial levels, trailing only 2024 and 2025.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Confirms 2026 is tracking within the recent record-hot cluster even before El Niño's full warming effect arrives.
insights.locator: Third-warmest start to a year

insights.claim: May and June 2026 were each the second-warmest respective month ever recorded, behind only 2024, while January 2026 was only the fourth- or fifth-warmest January as lingering weak La Niña conditions suppressed early-year temperatures — showing how quickly the year's ranking climbed as El Niño took hold.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Shows a month-by-month acceleration pattern likely to continue into the second half of 2026 as El Niño strengthens further.
insights.locator: January 2026 was only the fourth- or fifth-warmest

insights.claim: Copernicus reported that global sea-surface temperatures over ice-free oceans set a new June record in 2026.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Ocean-heat-content records provide independent confirmation of the warming signal beyond surface-air datasets, relevant to marine-heatwave and hurricane-season risk.
insights.locator: Meanwhile, Copernicus reported

insights.claim: Western Europe had its hottest June on record in 2026, at 3.05C above the 1991-2020 average, beating the record set only a year earlier, with a 22-30 June heat dome breaking 10 all-time national heat records and roughly 400 long-record station records.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Back-to-back annual European June heat records in 2025 and 2026 suggest the continent's summer warming trend is accelerating faster than global averages.
insights.locator: Western Europe had its hottest June

insights.claim: France set a new June national temperature record of 44.3C and the UK broke its June record on three consecutive days, reaching 37.3C, with the resulting humid heat driving an estimated death toll in the thousands.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Quantifies the human cost of the 2026 European heatwave, relevant to mortality-linked insurance and public-health cost modelling.
insights.locator: France set a new June national record

insights.claim: A separate heat dome brought record June temperatures to parts of North America in late June 2026, indicating the extreme heat was not confined to Europe.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Broadens the risk picture beyond Europe for agricultural and energy-demand forecasting in the second half of 2026.
insights.locator: A separate heat dome

themes.theme: 2026 projection: record odds vary sharply by dataset

insights.claim: Carbon Brief projects 2026 will finish around 1.51C above pre-industrial levels (90% range 1.45-1.57C), the second-warmest year on record behind 2024 (1.52C) and ahead of 2023 (1.43C) and 2025 (1.41C), with a 35% chance of surpassing 2024 as the outright warmest year.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete central case (second-warmest) plus tail probability (35%) for 2026's outcome, useful for weather-derivative or ESG-reporting purposes.
insights.locator: Carbon Brief estimates that 2026 will be

insights.claim: The probability that 2026 sets a new record varies drastically by dataset: roughly two-in-three for Berkeley Earth (66%) and NASA GISTEMP (65%), but only 35% for HadCRUT5, 24% for NOAA, and just 13% (ERA5) and 9% (JRA-3Q), reflecting how much of an outlier each dataset's 2024 reading already was.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Warns that 'will 2026 be a record year' headlines will depend heavily on which agency's dataset is cited, and a repeat of 2015's dataset-disagreement episode is likely.
insights.locator: Running the same projection gives odds

insights.claim: There is a 63% chance 2026 finishes above the 1.5C threshold, which would make it only the second calendar year after 2024 to average above 1.5C, though a single year above 1.5C does not itself constitute a breach of the Paris Agreement goal, which the IPCC defines as a 20-year average.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Clarifies that a hot single year is not equivalent to 'breaching Paris' in the technical sense, tempering headline risk from a 2026 1.5C reading.
insights.locator: It puts the chance that 2026 comes in above 1.5C

insights.claim: More than 30% of the global surface recorded a top-five warmest January-June start to a year in the ERA5 dataset, with 7.1% setting an outright record, while zero grid cells recorded a top-five coldest start, and in June alone 8.9% of the world's surface saw record warmth for the month.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Shows record warmth is broad-based across the planet rather than isolated hotspots, supporting the wider record-year probability case.
insights.locator: More than 30% of the global surface

insights.claim: Because El Niño's warming effect on global temperatures typically lags the tropical Pacific peak by about three months, the current El Niño, expected to peak in November-December 2026, will have its largest warming impact on 2027, mirroring the pattern seen after the 1997-98, 2015-16 and 2023-24 El Niño events.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Identifies 2027, not 2026, as the year most likely to deliver the standout temperature record, a forward-looking marker for climate-risk and commodity-weather positioning.
insights.locator: 2027 likely to be the warmest year in human history

insights.claim: Carbon Brief projects 2027 will come in around 1.71C above pre-industrial levels (90% range 1.49-1.93C), giving it a 92% chance of setting a new global temperature record and a 94% chance of exceeding 1.5C; combined, there is a 93% chance at least one of 2026 or 2027 sets a new record.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: The highest-confidence prediction in the piece: 2027 is Carbon Brief's base case for the next global temperature record, exceeding 2024 by nearly 0.2C.
insights.locator: This yields a best estimate for 2027

insights.claim: The long-term human-caused warming trend has accelerated from around 0.18C per decade in the early 2000s to around 0.27C per decade today.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Quantifies an accelerating underlying warming rate independent of El Niño/La Niña noise, a structural input for long-run climate-risk models.
insights.locator: The long-term warming trend

themes.theme: Arctic and Antarctic sea ice in record-low territory

insights.claim: Arctic sea ice has set or tied record daily lows on 39 days so far in 2026, following the joint-lowest winter maximum in the satellite era recorded in mid-March, with the most recent record-low days occurring in early July.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Tracks a parallel record-risk indicator alongside the temperature story, relevant to Arctic shipping-route and resource-access monitoring.
insights.locator: Arctic sea ice at record lows

insights.claim: Whether 2026 challenges 2012's record September Arctic sea-ice minimum will be determined by conditions over the following two months, since early-summer ice extent is a poor predictor of the September minimum.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Flags a specific near-term window (August-September 2026) to watch for a potential new Arctic sea-ice record.
insights.locator: The trajectory over the coming two months

insights.claim: Antarctic sea ice has stayed below the 1979-2010 historical range for nearly all of 2026 and is currently about 300,000km2 below that envelope, but it has remained clear of the record lows set in 2023 and has not set any new daily records this year.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Distinguishes Antarctic ice, below average but not record-breaking, from the Arctic's more extreme record-low trajectory, a nuance for polar-risk trackers.
insights.locator: Antarctic sea ice, meanwhile
